items.title: The Satavahanas in Andhra — the Eastern Dimension
items.body:
## Andhras of the Puranas

- The **Puranas call the Satavahana rulers the 'Andhras'**, and their long rule (c.2nd century BCE–3rd century CE) laid the foundation of Andhra's classical culture.
- While **Pratishthana (Paithan)** on the Godavari was the western capital, **Dhanyakataka** (with the fortified township of **Dharanikota**, adjacent to Amaravati on the Krishna) was the great **eastern centre** in coastal Andhra.

## Culture and trade

- The lower Krishna–Godavari delta was the richest part of the realm — a hub of **maritime trade** (muslin/cotton textiles prized by Rome) through Andhra ports.
- The court patronised **Prakrit literature**: king **Hala's Gatha Saptasati** and **Gunadhya's Brihatkatha** (in Paisachi Prakrit) belong to this milieu.
- Above all, the Satavahana era made Andhra the **cradle of Indian Buddhist art**, seen at Amaravati.

> Note: this note deliberately covers the *Andhra* angle; the pan-India Satavahana political narrative (Simuka, Gautamiputra Satakarni vs Nahapana, Nasik Prashasti) is treated separately under Ancient India.
keyPoints: The Puranas call the Satavahanas the 'Andhras'.
Western capital = Pratishthana (Paithan); eastern centre = Dhanyakataka/Dharanikota near Amaravati.
Krishna-Godavari delta drove maritime trade, exporting textiles to Rome.
Court Prakrit literature: Hala's Gatha Saptasati and Gunadhya's Brihatkatha (Paisachi).
Satavahana era = cradle of the Amaravati school of Buddhist art.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi); Wikipedia — Satavahana dynasty (verified)

items.title: Amaravati Stupa & the Amaravati School of Art
items.body:
## The Mahachaitya

- The **Amaravati Stupa (Mahachaitya)** in **Palnadu district** was built and enlarged in phases between about the **3rd century BCE and c.250 CE**, flourishing under the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus.
- Distinctive Andhra features: the hemispherical **anda (dome)**, a great **railing** carved with reliefs, and sets of **five ayaka pillars** on platforms at each of the four cardinal projections.
- It is protected by the **ASI**; many carved marbles are now in the **Government Museum, Chennai** and the **British Museum** (the 'Amaravati Marbles'), a legacy of Colin Mackenzie's early surveys.

## The art school

- Amaravati is one of the **three great early schools** of Indian sculpture, alongside **Gandhara** (grey schist, Hellenistic) and **Mathura** (red sandstone).
- Its hallmark is **crowded, dynamic narrative relief** in **white-greenish limestone**, illustrating Jataka stories and the Buddha's life — first with symbols, later in human form.
- The style radiated outward, shaping Buddhist art in **Sri Lanka and South-East Asia**.

| School | Material | Region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gandhara | grey schist | NW frontier |
| Mathura | red sandstone | Uttar Pradesh |
| Amaravati | white limestone | Krishna valley, Andhra |
keyPoints: Amaravati Mahachaitya (Palnadu dist.) built in phases c.3rd c BCE-250 CE, ASI-protected.
Andhra stupa signature = five ayaka pillars on each of the four sides.
Amaravati is one of three great early schools with Gandhara and Mathura.
Medium = white-greenish limestone; style = crowded narrative Jataka reliefs.
Amaravati art influenced Sri Lanka and South-East Asia; marbles now in Chennai and the British Museum.
items.mnemonic: Three schools by stone = 'G-schist, M-sandstone, A-limestone' (Gandhara, Mathura, Amaravati).
items.source: Wikipedia — Amaravati Stupa; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: The Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)
items.body:
## Successors of the Satavahanas

- The **Andhra Ikshvakus** ruled the **eastern Krishna valley** for over a century in the **3rd–4th centuries CE**, from their capital **Vijayapuri** in the **Nagarjunakonda** valley.
- They are called *Andhra Ikshvakus* / *Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri* to distinguish them from the legendary solar-dynasty Ikshvakus of Kosala.

## Rulers

- Succession: **Vasishthiputra Chamtamula (founder)** → **Virapurushadatta** → **Ehuvala Chamtamula** → **Rudrapurushadatta (last)**.
- They kept the Satavahana-style **matronymics** (e.g. Vasishthiputra).

## A divided religious household

- The **kings remained Brahmanical**, performing **Vedic sacrifices** (agnihotra, vajapeya, ashvamedha).
- The **royal women** — most famously the princess **Chamtisiri** — were **generous Buddhist patrons**, funding the Mahachaitya and monasteries at Nagarjunakonda. This royal-Vedic / feminine-Buddhist split is a favourite exam point.
keyPoints: Ikshvakus ruled the eastern Krishna valley (3rd-4th c CE) from Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda).
Called Andhra Ikshvakus to distinguish them from the Ikshvakus of Kosala.
Ruler order: Chamtamula (founder) -> Virapurushadatta -> Ehuvala Chamtamula -> Rudrapurushadatta.
Kings performed Vedic sacrifices (ashvamedha); they retained matronymics.
Royal women (e.g. Chamtisiri) were the great Buddhist patrons of Nagarjunakonda.
items.source: Wikipedia — Ikshvaku dynasty (Andhra); History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: Nagarjunakonda, Acharya Nagarjuna & Andhra Buddhism
items.body:
## Nagarjunakonda

- Named after **Acharya Nagarjuna**, the valley was a major Buddhist campus of **mahachaityas, viharas and study-halls**, plus a rare **stadium/amphitheatre**.
- Excavations revealed a **monastery for monks from Sri Lanka** — evidence that Andhra was a launch-point for Buddhism's spread to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.
- When the **Nagarjuna Sagar dam** reservoir was created, the monuments were **submerged**; the threatened relics were **excavated and re-erected on a hilltop that is now an island museum**.

## Acharya Nagarjuna

- Founder of the **Madhyamika** (middle-path) school and its doctrine of **Sunyavada** (emptiness); author of the **Mula-madhyamaka-karika**.
- Tradition links him to **Sriparvata** (the Nagarjunakonda–Srisailam hills); his dialectic influenced later Indian philosophy, including Sankara's Advaita.

## Andhra — a Buddhist heartland

- The **Buddha is traditionally said to have preached the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka**.
- The **Mahasanghika-derived Chaitika (Andhaka) schools** were strong in the Krishna valley, and the **cult of Avalokitesvara** is believed to have originated in Andhra.
- Buddhism flourished for over a millennium and declined from about the **6th century CE**.
keyPoints: Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri) had mahachaityas, viharas and a monastery for Sri Lankan monks.
Its monuments were submerged by the Nagarjuna Sagar dam and moved to an island museum.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school (Sunyavada); wrote the Mula-madhyamaka-karika.
Buddha traditionally preached the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka.
Andhaka/Chaitika (Mahasanghika) schools and the Avalokitesvara cult are linked to Andhra; decline from c.6th c CE.
items.source: Wikipedia — Nagarjunakonda / Nagarjuna; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: Buddhist Sites of Andhra — a Map
items.body:
## Andhra's Buddhist geography

Andhra has one of India's **densest clusters of ancient Buddhist sites**, spanning Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana phases.

| Site | Location | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amaravati | Palnadu (Krishna) | Mahachaitya; Amaravati art school |
| Nagarjunakonda | Palnadu (Krishna) | Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri |
| Bhattiprolu | Bapatla/Guntur | relic caskets; Bhattiprolu Brahmi script |
| Salihundam | Srikakulam (Vamsadhara) | Kalinga site; all three phases |
| Guntupalli | West Godavari | early rock-cut chaitya (also early Jain caves) |
| Ghantasala | Krishna | stupa + ancient port |
| Jaggayyapeta | Krishna valley | early relief sculpture |
| Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram | near Visakhapatnam | hill-top monasteries |
| Ramatirtham | Vizianagaram | Buddhist and Jain remains |

## Bhattiprolu's special place

- Its inscribed **relic caskets** give **one of the earliest specimens of Brahmi in South India** — the **Bhattiprolu script**, regarded as an ancestor of the Telugu–Kannada script family.
- **Salihundam**, on the south bank of the **Vamsadhara** near Kalingapatnam, shows the full **Hinayana → Mahayana → Vajrayana** evolution in the Kalinga borderland.
keyPoints: Andhra has one of India's densest clusters of ancient Buddhist sites.
Krishna-valley core: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli.
Visakhapatnam hill monasteries: Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram (Bojjannakonda).
Bhattiprolu relic caskets = early southern Brahmi (Bhattiprolu script), ancestor of Telugu-Kannada.
Salihundam (Srikakulam, Vamsadhara) shows Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana phases.
items.source: Wikipedia — Bhattiprolu / Salihundam; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: Salankayanas & Vishnukundins — the Vengi Successors
items.body:
## Salankayanas of Vengi (c.300–440 CE)

- Ruled the **Godavari–Krishna doab** from **Vengi (Pedavegi, near Eluru)** after the Ikshvakus.
- Used the **bull (Nandi)** as their dynastic emblem; at first feudatories of the Pallavas, later independent, and finally displaced by the Vishnukundins.

## Vishnukundins (5th–7th c CE)

- **Madhava Varma** was the greatest ruler, credited with **Vedic sacrifices including the ashvamedha**; the dynasty **wrested coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas** and is linked with capitals such as **Denduluru** and the **Amaravati/Keesaragutta** region.
- Their rule ended when **Pulakeshin II** (Badami Chalukya) conquered the eastern Deccan and installed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** — founder of the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (from 624 CE)**.
- The **early rock-cut cave temples** at **Undavalli** (monolithic reclining Vishnu), **Mogalrajapuram** and **Bhairavakonda** are ascribed to this period.

## The thread of succession

Dhanyakataka (Satavahanas) → Vijayapuri (Ikshvakus) → **Vengi** (Salankayanas → Vishnukundins) → Eastern Chalukyas — the political nucleus of coastal Andhra steadily shifted to Vengi.
keyPoints: Salankayanas (c.300-440 CE) ruled the Godavari-Krishna doab from Vengi (Pedavegi); bull emblem.
Vishnukundins (5th-7th c CE) took coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas; greatest king Madhava Varma (ashvamedha).
Vishnukundin rule ended by Chalukya Pulakeshin II, who installed Kubja Vishnuvardhana -> Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE).
Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda cave temples belong to the Vishnukundi period.
Political centre shifted: Dhanyakataka -> Vijayapuri -> Vengi -> Eastern Chalukyas.
items.source: Wikipedia — Salankayana / Vishnukundina dynasties; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified
